chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from a man from our companions from Abu al-Subbah al-Kinani said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'We have a neighbor from Hamdan, called Al-Ja'd ibn Abdillah, who sits with us. When we mention Ali, Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him), and his virtues, he speaks ill of him. Should I seek your permission regarding him?' He said, 'Did you mean to do it?' I said, 'Yes, by God, if you give me permission, I will lie in wait for him. When he comes out, I will leap upon him with my sword and strike him until I kill him.'

He said, 'O Abu al-Subbah, this is al-fatk (sudden, surprise attack). The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) has forbidden al-fatk. O Abu al-Subbah, indeed Islam has restrained al-fatk. But leave him, and you will be sufficient with another (person to kill him).'

Abu al-Subbah said: When I returned from Medina to Kufa, I did not stay there for more than eighteen days. I went out to the mosque and prayed Fajr, then I lingered (after prayer). Suddenly, a man was nudging me with his foot. He said, 'O Abu al-Subbah, good tidings!' I said, 'May God bless you with good, what is it?' He said, 'Indeed, Al-Ja'd ibn Abdillah spent the night in his house which is in the graveyard. They woke him for prayer, and behold, he was like a blown leather bag, dead. So they went to carry him, and his flesh was falling off his bones. They gathered him in a skin, and beneath him was black, so they buried him.'

key_terms.أَمِيرُ اَلْمُؤُمِنِينَ: Commander of the Faithful (title for Imam Ali)
key_terms.اَلزِّقُّ: A leather bag, often used to describe a body swollen or stiff after death

ai.seo_question: What is the meaning of 'al-fatk' in the context of killing a neighbor who speaks ill of the Imams?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) grants Abu al-Subbah permission to kill his neighbor Al-Ja'd for backbiting Imam Ali, but corrects his violent method of 'al-fatk' (sudden ambush) to align with Prophetic tradition, implying divine removal rather than human vengeance. The narrative concludes with Al-Ja'd’s sudden death in his home, described as being like a 'blown leather bag' with flesh falling off, which Shia scholars view as a miraculous sign of God's protection of the Ahl al-Bayt's honor and the efficacy of patient endurance (sabr).
